item.title: Nepali City Struggles to Handle the Many Bodies on Its Riverbanks
item.description:
A city in Nepal has received far more bodies than its morgues can accommodate.

Bharatpur, the headquarters of Chitwan district, lies downstream from the devastated sites of the floods that killed hundreds of people this week, with many more still unaccounted for. The district has become the main collection point for bodies that were caught in the initial torrent of floodwaters, or that have been floating to the banks of the Bhotekoshi River since.

By Friday afternoon, the remains of about 220 people had washed down to the district, according to Nepal’s disaster management authority. But the morgues at hospitals across Chitwan can barely house three dozen bodies, Rameshwor Poudel, the district’s police chief, said in a phone interview.

On Saturday, the authorities in Chitwan said they would bury those remains, still unidentified, because they were decomposing and posed a health risk.

The town had been relying on a government building that the Nepali authorities had turned into a makeshift mortuary for about 150 bodies, Mr. Poudel said on Friday, as they were trying to arrange for dry ice to help preserve them.

“It has no chilling facilities,” he said of the hall. “It only has air-conditioners.”

At least two other districts in Nepal have reported similar difficulties in storing such large numbers of remains.

The devastating flooding has stretched government resources in Nepal, a deeply poor country where hospitals and infrastructure already had limited capacity. Resources have been strained even in Bharatpur, a transportation hub that connects much of Nepal to the road network leading to the capital, Kathmandu.

Mr. Poudel said dozens of bodies had been pulled up to the riverbank in pieces, making identification difficult. Before burying them, the authorities will preserve DNA samples so that families can later claim any remains that are identified, Chitwan’s district administration said.

Before the decision to bury the bodies was made, Mr. Poudel said the police were cleaning and taking pictures of them. If one was recognizable, they posted photographs outside the hall so that people searching for missing relatives could have a first look.

As of Friday afternoon, he said, two bodies had been identified and handed over to families.

One of them was Kabir Lal Chaudhary, 23. He was working for a hydropower company more than 100 miles upstream when he was swept away by the flood.

Mr. Chaudhary’s brother, Sugrib Tharu, said he had waited for two hours at the temporary morgue in Bharatpur before the authorities handed over his remains.

“The body is decaying,” Mr. Tharu said by phone, as he traveled home in an ambulance. “If there had been a chilling facility, it would have been in a better condition.”

Mujib Mashal contributed reporting.

item.title: See the Moments After a Himalayan Glacier Collapsed, Causing a Deadly Flood
item.description:
They heard the avalanche before they saw it.

Ziha Yitie, a tour guide, and his group of hikers had spent Wednesday morning climbing to an observation deck in Tibet with a view of snow-capped mountains across the border in Nepal.

Mr. Ziha, 26, said a break in the morning mist uncovered Tsangbu Ri’s dramatic peak and glacier. They pulled out their cameras.

As they filmed, the hikers heard a series of deep rumbles. They dismissed the sounds as thunder. Then, just after 10:50 a.m. in Tibet, a loud crack shot through the valley.

“It sounded like explosives detonating inside the mountains,” Mr. Ziha said. For several minutes after the initial sound, he said, they were hit with a wall of noise from an avalanche.

A comparison of the hikers’ footage before and after the avalanche offers the clearest view yet of the scale of the glacial ice and rock that dropped into a valley below.

But it wasn’t until the group descended that they saw blocked roads and heard news reports of the devastation caused by the avalanche and subsequent flood.

Another hiker captured the moments immediately after the glacier collapsed. His video shows dust and debris racing into the valley below.

item.title: Nepal’s Hydropower Industry Was Booming. Now 900 Workers Are Missing.
item.description:
The work was always dangerous, demanding long hours digging tunnels in a region prone to natural disasters.

But Nepal’s hydroelectric industry attracted poor laborers and highly trained engineers alike, as investments poured in from across Asia.

Now, hundreds of workers are missing after a deadly flood tore through 14 hydropower projects concentrated along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli Rivers, near Nepal’s border with Tibet.

As counts of the dead and missing continue to grow, over 900 people from the hydropower projects are unaccounted for, according to Nepal’s disaster relief agency, bringing the total number of missing people to over 1,900.

Videos have shown rescuers pulling survivors from thick mud that filled hydropower tunnels, and many fear that others are dead or trapped inside.

“Many engineers are probably dead,” said Dinesh Paudel, a geographer at Appalachian State University who has studied development in Nepal. He said on Friday that he had yet to hear from a friend who worked on one of the hydropower projects.

The flood on Wednesday swallowed buildings, washed away bridges and severely damaged hydropower facilities, which generate electricity as water moves rapidly downstream.

Despite the region’s susceptibility to natural disasters, including earthquakes, floods and landslides, its hydropower industry has boomed over the last decade.

Because of the region’s access to plenty of water running down steep rivers and its proximity to China, the river corridor in northern Nepal’s Rasuwa district is one of the country’s largest and most active sites of hydropower projects, drawing new workers to the rural Himalayas, experts said.

“The river has all the ingredients,” said Dr. Paudel. “And once you have hydropower in one location, it’s easier to put another. The infrastructure and roads are built.”

A handful of hydropower projects in the Rasuwa district are listed as having “under construction licenses” by Nepal’s Independent Power Producers’ Association. Dr. Paudel said construction and final testing would draw more workers to the sites.

Such sites are often built by Chinese companies and staffed by poor Nepali laborers, including many who traveled from other parts of the country without the means to seek better work abroad, Dr. Paudel said.

The job can involve maintaining and digging tunnels, often with pickaxes, said Galen Murton, a geographer at James Madison University who has studied Nepal’s infrastructure.

“There’s highly educated, sophisticated engineers,” Dr. Murton said. “It’s a diverse population.”

“But the guys doing the hardest work come from the most hardscrabble backgrounds,” he added.

The hydropower projects had brought people to northern Nepal and spun off a local economy around it, Dr. Murton said. But it’s unclear what remains of it now.

“Disasters have damaged hydropower facilities before,” Dr. Murton said. “But I can’t think of a singular event where things were there and then it was gone.”

Rebecca L. Davis contributed reporting.

item.title: In the Age of Global Warming, Some Fear ‘the Entire Himalayas Are Melting’
item.description:
On Wednesday morning, part of a glacier and the mountainside beneath it collapsed on the north side of Langtang Lirung, a 23,734-foot peak near Nepal’s border with Tibet, setting off a 60-mile flood of water, mud and debris.

By Friday, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said that 579 people had been killed. Many, many more are still missing.

More than 4,000 miles west, victims of another disaster in the region were being mourned. That morning, in Dorset, England, family and friends gathered to commemorate Nirmal Purja, the celebrated Nepali mountaineer known as Nimsdai. Among them was Mingma Gyalje Sherpa, one of Nepal’s leading climbers and the founder of the expedition company Imagine Nepal. After an avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan’s Karakoram range killed Mr. Purja and nine other climbers on July 30, Mr. Mingma Sherpa led the expedition that recovered Mr. Purja’s body.

The two disasters occurred within a month of each other on the mountainous region that extends from Pakistan through Nepal, where scientists, climbers and trekkers have witnessed accelerating losses of snow and ice.

For Nepal, the consequences extend far beyond the mountains. Tourism represents 6.1 percent of the country’s economy and supported about 1.2 million jobs in 2023, roughly 15 percent of all employment, according to the World Bank.

Of the more than 1.16 million international visitors who went to Nepal in 2025, 165,056 listed trekking and mountaineering as their primary reason for visiting. The industry that has grown around them includes more than 3,000 trekking agencies and tens of thousands of registered guides, as well as expedition companies, porters, cooks, teahouses, hotels, airlines, helicopter operators and drivers.

At the lucrative extreme is high-altitude climbing. This spring, 1,195 climbers obtained permits for 31 mountains, generating about $9 million in government royalties alone. Nearly 500 received permits for Mount Everest, where the spring permit for a foreign climber now costs $15,000.

Over seven years working on expeditions, Mr. Purja had become one of the world’s best-known climbers and the owner of an international expedition company, Elite Exped, with his own sports clothing line. Mr. Mingma Sherpa is part of the same generation. His company runs expeditions on Everest and other Himalayan peaks. “It’s one of the best jobs in Nepal,” he said, speaking after the Langtang Lirung flood. A successful high-altitude guide, he estimated, can make “10 times” an ordinary Nepali salary.

But many believe that this livelihood is threatened by global warming. Arbindra Khadka, 35, a glaciologist and research scientist at Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu, noted that Himalayan glaciers are losing about a meter (nearly 3.3 feet) of ice a year. “It’s not just Everest” that is in trouble, he said. “The entire Himalayas are melting.”

Increasingly, those in the trekking business depend on mountains that are changing beneath climbers’ feet. Tul Singh Gurung, president of the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association, believes the Broad Peak avalanche may have begun when a serac, a tower of glacial ice, collapsed and triggered the slab avalanche below. What troubled him was where it happened. Climbers generally regarded the slope between Camps II and III as one of Broad Peak’s more stable sections at that time of year.

“The mountains are getting black,” Mr. Gurung said, describing the disappearing snow and ice across the Himalayas and Karakoram. “Every mountain has a rockfall problem.”

Dave Watson, a 50-year-old American mountaineer who has summited Mount Everest seven times since 2004, has witnessed the change. “Some of this hazard has always been there, but in a lower volume,” Mr. Watson said.

The changes are visible not just at the extreme elevations reached by Everest climbers but also on mountains visited by the trekkers and climbers vital to Nepal’s economy.

Dr. Khadka cautioned that it was too early to say precisely what triggered the Langtang disaster. But he theorized that a relatively small cornice collapse high on the ridges of Langtang Lirung had started an avalanche of loose rock and moraine across slippery, thawing ground during the wet mid-monsoon season.

For Dr. Khadka, the latest disaster is personal. Speaking from Nepal, he was waiting for news of missing relatives and friends.

Mr. Gurung said guides were already encountering places where traditional climbing and trekking routes had become difficult to recognize as snow and ice disappear and bare rock emerges. One of the most closely watched is the Khumbu Icefall, which begins the climbing route up Everest from Nepal. Dr. Khadka expects it to keep changing. Some sections may become easier to cross, he said, while hanging ice and exposed slopes create new dangers.

Mr. Mingma Sherpa has watched the transformation firsthand. When he first crossed the Icefall in 2004, he remembers negotiating numerous crevasses on aluminum ladders. This year, he said, climbers needed ladders in only two places.

Mr. Watson knew the region devastated by the latest flood. He passed through the Nepal-Tibet border area twice in 2024 and remembered how dramatically it had developed since his early expeditions two decades ago. On journeys to the north side of Everest, crossing the border used to require an overnight stop while climbers waited for immigration formalities and transferred equipment between trucks. In recent years, roads, restaurants, hotels and residences have been built to cater to increasing traffic between the two countries.

Mr. Watson saw the aftermath of another Himalayan catastrophe. An earthquake in 2015 shook loose rock and ice in Langtang, where an avalanche buried much of the village and killed hundreds. “The thousand-year flood is happening every few years now,” he said.

Yet Nepal’s younger climbers show little sign of abandoning the profession. Mr. Mingma Sherpa said young people continued to be drawn by the pay and the work, although their backgrounds are changing. Increasingly, Sherpa families live in Kathmandu and other lower-altitude cities. “We were used to playing at higher altitude,” he said. “Now Sherpas are born in the city.”

Dipan Gurung, 25, is part of the new generation of guides. He comes from the Makalu region and a family of farmers rather than the Khumbu communities traditionally associated with Himalayan guiding. He began as a trekking porter in 2019. Many young men from his region traditionally went into the army, he said; now growing numbers are seeking professional climbing and rescue training.

Mr. Gurung has watched glaciers melt into ponds. “We are facing a future of rockfalls and floods,” he said. Yet he does not believe that makes his career prohibitively dangerous. While the mountains are becoming less predictable, equipment and tools are more accurate and advanced. His generation has detailed weather forecasts, GPS devices, avalanche transceivers, lighter equipment and training in reading snowpacks. They also use drones, which provide information on conditions and carry supplies.

Some of those tools are already changing the way Everest is climbed, particularly for the Sherpas and other Nepali high-altitude workers who have long borne much of the danger of commercial expeditions. While foreign clients may cross the Khumbu Icefall a handful of times during an expedition, Nepali workers traditionally make repeated trips through it, carrying tents, oxygen, food and equipment to higher camps. On April 18, 2014, that disparity in risk became starkly apparent when a mass of ice collapsed above the route, killing 16 Nepali climbing workers in the icefall.

Drones now offer a way to reduce some of that exposure. “We are trying to reduce people going through the icefall by moving loads up by drones,” Mr. Gurung said, describing machines capable of carrying roughly 88 pounds. Mr. Watson expects drones to increasingly scout for danger as well. “Drones will be a huge part of safety plans in the future,” he said.

Helicopters offer another way around dangerous terrain, although Mr. Gurung and Mr. Watson are wary of treating them as a solution because high-altitude flying depends on visibility, wind and landing conditions.

On Wednesday, while Mr. Purja’s family and friends gathered in England, Mr. Gurung was back at work in Nepal, helping coordinate rescue teams in the disaster zone. With roads severed and some areas accessible only by helicopter, his association was sending trained guides into steep terrain and confined spaces difficult for conventional rescue teams to reach.

Soon, if conditions allow, climbers and trekkers will return to the mountains. The autumn trekking season is approaching. Expeditions are booked, and guides, porters, teahouses and lodges are depending on them.

For Mr. Watson, perhaps the starkest evidence of how much those mountains have changed is at the very top of the world.

“If the summit of Everest has that much less ice,” Mr. Watson said, “then there is no place on Earth that is untouched.”

item.title: Fast Forward
item.description:
The cursed island town in the horror-comedy series “Widow’s Bay” is so remote that there’s no Wi-Fi and cell service is unreliable. This means residents are left to landlines and walkie-talkies to communicate. These limitations not only add to the feeling of creepy isolation, but they also dispense with the modern challenge of depicting smartphone usage onscreen. When Mayor Tom Loftis wants to talk to someone, he must call them using the multi-line phone in his office or the rotary model affixed to his kitchen wall.

Nostalgia for outmoded technology is bittersweet: We can’t imagine life without present-day conveniences, but things were so much simpler before! Our understanding of the world was slow to update. We said we’d meet at the restaurant at 6, and you couldn’t switch the location at the last minute or change the time if you were running late. We settled on the route we’d take to drive from A to B, no GPS to change it with a few seconds’ notice because of the traffic jam ahead. No moment-to-moment updates from friends, no impulse-Googling the name of that shampoo or tomorrow’s weather, no asking Claude. Our brains contained a certain amount of knowledge, and we didn’t add to it without time and effort.

In The Times today, Kera Bolonik writes about the mix tape, that relic of another era, which “took time, thought, careful listening and a level of physical coordination beyond what goes into the making of a Spotify playlist.” Good mix-tape-makers were experts in manipulating the pause and record buttons on the hi-fi, engaging with the equipment to create a tangible artifact. Unlike a playlist, tapes were material, present in the landscape. It made sense that something so meaningful took up room in the world.

“You have to imagine a space where music was a rumor,” the writer Jonathan Lethem told Kera. “You might hear something and not be able to know what it was, and no one can tell you, and it’s driving you crazy.” In the Shazam-less past, you’d hear a song and have no way to instantly entrap it. You’d live with the memory of the song you heard, hoping to catch it again on the radio. I remember becoming enamored of a song I heard on the radio in France in 1995 and telling my boyfriend back home that I’d heard the best new David Bowie track. There was no new Bowie album that we knew about, but we asked the clerks in every record store about it all the same. It would be six months before it came out in the States, and we discovered it wasn’t a Bowie song at all, but “A Girl Like You” by the Scottish musician Edwyn Collins. I put it on every mix tape I made that year.

There’s a whole universe of pared-back gadgets for those who miss the simplicity of old tech: dumbphones, internet-connected typewriters, screen-free digital cameras. There are apps that take a long time to send texts. But there’s something unsatisfying about using tech to address over-technification. Perhaps the answer lies in the technology that has persisted in its unimprovable simplicity: A pad and paper have never failed to save my journal entries or added formatting I didn’t ask for. I treasure my wristwatch that I never have to charge, the digital alarm clock that shows me the time from across the room.

I no longer have the dual-cassette boom box on which I made countless mixes, but Maxell released a Bluetooth cassette player this year. I don’t love the idea of buying something new in order to capture the magic of something old, but that something old might be worth pursuing. As Kera wrote: “More than just relics, mix tapes are portals to specific moments. Perhaps even more than old photos, they reanimate the past.”

Trump Administration

The U.S. reached a deal to take majority control of a huge portion of Venezuela’s oil reserves, President Trump announced last night. The deal is for more than 65 billion barrels of oil — almost as much as all of the proven reserves in the United States.

The Trump administration has proposed giving a parcel of public land in Yosemite National Park to a private developer.

ICE has arrested Milo Yiannopoulos, the British right-wing agitator and early Trump supporter. He faces possible deportation after overstaying his visa.

More Politics

Wyoming’s governor, a Republican, said he was concerned by the “very odd” behavior of federal election monitors who tried to interview voters and examine voting machines during the state’s primaries last week.

It looks as though a New York Jet will finally win something: A former kicker, Jay Feely, is running against a former sideline doctor, Amish Shah, in a House race in Arizona.

The Times analyzed thousands of donations this midterms season and made a leaderboard of the top 20 biggest donors. It’s dominated by tech figures and Republicans.

Nepal Floods

At least 1,900 people are missing after the devastating flash flood in the Himalayas, officials now say, roughly twice as many as previously estimated.

New video shows how a giant glacier broke away from a mountain ridge, sending floodwaters crashing through valleys below. Watch The Times’s exclusive footage.

Around the World

The Taliban have banned education for millions of Afghan girls. Times journalists examined the secret classrooms where some are defying the rules.

Iranians are increasingly desperate six months into the war with the United States. Even some who initially cheered Trump’s intervention now fear a failing economy.

Other Big Stories

In his first speech before the Fed’s annual conference in Jackson, Wyo., the new chair, Kevin Warsh, said the central bank was chiefly focused on getting inflation down. Investors expect interest rates to rise.

A judge ruled that a key confession by Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, accused of plotting the Sept. 11 attacks, was not voluntary and must be excluded from his trial.

Dolly Parton

Everyone knows Dolly as a consummate singer and songwriter. But she was also a prolific philanthropist whose gifts supported wildlife conservation and the development of the Covid-19 vaccine, among other things.

The crown jewel of her philanthropic efforts was the Imagination Library, which has given children hundreds of millions of free books.

Tim Curry

Curry’s performance as Dr. Frank-N-Furter, the cross-dressing mad scientist of “The Rocky Horror Show,” helped bring androgynous fashion into the mainstream.

Along with being extraordinarily funny, Curry was a superlative storyteller. A writer who interviewed him three times last year reflects on what it was like to talk with him.

Yayoi Kusama

In her long life, Kusama achieved something rare: two very different moments of stardom, almost as though she’d been two different artists, our critic writes.

Kusama created a hugely varied oeuvre — abstract paintings, fabric phalluses, naked performance pieces … you name it. See her life in pictures.

Grand Theft Auto VI, the series’ first entry in over a decade, is due out in November. It’s a rare monocultural moment, akin to the release of a new Beyoncé album or Martin Scorsese film. Our reporter visited the studio in Edinburgh where it’s being made.

In “Coyote vs. Acme,” a new live action-animation hybrid in theaters this weekend, Wile E. Coyote sues the company behind those gadgets that always seem to backfire. It’s “a terrifically daffy film,” our critic writes.

Rupert Grint, who starred as Ron Weasley in all eight “Harry Potter” films, will reprise the role in “Harry Potter and the Cursed Child” on Broadway.

“Paranormal Activity,” the horror film series, is now haunting Broadway. Our theater critic says it “feels like watching a magic show on a roller coaster.”

By Melissa Clark

Have you made ratatouille yet this year? Fear not — there are still a few weeks of eggplant-zucchini-pepper-tomato season left to go before the pumpkins take over. In my riff on the Provençal classic, I roast the vegetables separately on sheet pans to soften and brown them, then combine them for a final, olive oil-coated bake that lets them practically melt. Served with fresh goat cheese and a warm baguette, it’s one of my favorite meatless meals.

The Hunt: A costume supervisor for TV and film productions wanted a home in Portland, Ore., with a yard and a spare bedroom for visitors. Which house did he choose? Play our game.

What you get for $725,000: An American Foursquare in Providence, R.I.; a Spanish-style house in Tulsa, Okla.; and a two-story house in Salt Lake City. See them all.

Tree-huggers: In Red Hook, Brooklyn, developers spent $400,000 to ensure their new project didn’t disturb a six-story maple tree already on the lot.

Ask Real Estate: My neighbor installed a camera pointing at my yard. Is that legal?

New boosters: The F.D.A. approved updated Covid vaccines this week. Here’s what you need to know about the shots.

Elective M.R.I.s: Celebrities are raving about full-body scans. But researchers say that healthy people don’t need them — and that they can lead to more harm than good.

Baby on board: Traveling while pregnant is possible, but there are some risks. It’s wise to plan ahead.

In fashion, what goes around comes around. Take culottes: These mid-calf, wide-leg pants have gone in and out of style for decades. Today, all signs point to a culotte revival, and I have a few tips to help you find a timeless pair. Go for something that feels familiar, like a khaki-esque pair that could match T-shirts, button-ups, sweaters or cardigans. One of my favorite pairs has sumptuous legs and immaculate pleats. They’re hard to ignore, yes, but they’re easy to style year-round. In warmer weather, they look great with heeled sandals. For fall, why not try them with cowboy boots? (Another classic!) — Frances Solá-Santiago

item.title: Elbows and Chin Up: A Whirlwind Week in the U.S.-Canada Trade War
item.description:
For the past two weeks we have worked closely with our Washington colleagues to get the most detailed, corroborated account of what happened when weeks of trade talks between Canada and the United States broke down late last Friday night.

Saturday morning brought a rallying speech from Prime Minister Mark Carney, and the two countries are now locked into a trade war. President Trump restarted his rhetorical attacks on Canada’s sovereignty and signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” a decision derided, mocked and shrugged off by Canadians and others. What comes next?

We worked with The Times’s trade reporter Ana Swanson in Washington, and between us we spoke to two U.S. government officials and three Canadian officials with direct knowledge of the talks, as well as two former U.S. officials and five industry leaders on both sides of the border who were briefed throughout.

We put each side’s claims to the other and found that, fundamentally, there were no major discrepancies between the two narratives, despite the heightened political tensions in the days after.

Our key findings, corroborated by officials on both sides of the negotiating table:

Talks were positive up until Tuesday night. Mr. Carney offered to collaborate on the Keystone XL pipeline, which delighted Mr. Trump. By the end of the week that was off the table.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was a factor in destabilizing the talks as he intervened repeatedly, including on Wednesday and Friday, to push for tariffs on steel, autos and auto parts, all of which fall under his purview.

The United States insisted on maintaining the freedom to change its tariff policy on Canada without a dispute resolution mechanism or warning built into the new agreement. It also asked for Canada to notify and coordinate with the U.S. on steel tariffs that Canada enforces on other trading partners.

Mr. Carney spoke with Premier Doug Ford of Ontario minutes before he pulled the plug on the talks.

Much has been made of the French-language issue as a dividing line in the talks. Our reporting shows that the U.S. side did advance a demand for Canada to amend or repeal laws that protect Canadian content by asking streaming platforms to surface it more prominently for Canadian users. The U.S. side said that it wasn’t a red line for them.

The U.S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer, told Ana Swanson that, in terms of stable and official concessions, the United States was offering the best deal of any country in the world.

Canada’s Conservatives are pressing Mr. Carney to release the text of the agreement he refused to sign. Our reporting shows that the two negotiating teams signed confidentiality agreements (a requirement that is apparently standard in Trump administrations). Additionally our sources told us that the text was constantly changing, meaning that a draft would not necessarily reflect exactly where the latest point of agreement was, even if the confidentiality agreement was to be ignored.

Here’s a gift link to the story, and a link directly below if you already subscribe to The Times.

To help you make sense of a dizzying week in the trade war, we’ve pulled all our coverage into the Canada Letter as a special report.

Economists this week expect that the new measures won’t shrink Canada’s economy very much. But for individual businesses that depend on exporting to the United States, the 50 percent tariffs may be a disaster. The economy is sheltered because Mr. Trump left some of Canada’s most valuable exports off his hit list, including oil, gas and potash. What’s on the U.S. list? Some odd things.

Canada retaliated with tariffs on about 700 American products. But that quickly underscored how difficult it is to make sure that trade revenge doesn’t backfire. The government was quickly forced to pull dozens of fish and fish products off the list after Canadian fishing groups, whose industry is closely integrated with the United States, warned that the measure would hurt them equally.

Then, on Friday, came data that indicated Mr. Trump had failed to cripple Canada’s economy: About a year and a half after he put tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos, the Canadian economy grew by an equivalent one-year rate of 3.3 percent in the second quarter of this year. Statistics Canada said that was driven by a boost in exports and increased auto production.

The first wave of tariffs against Canada last year provoked a grass-roots effort to support all things local and shun the United States. Since then, Canada has inked new deals, notably on autos and energy, with countries in Asia and Europe that have put it on a stronger economic footing.

Still, business owners in areas targeted by Mr. Trump’s tariffs expect to hurt financially. Some are embracing the show of resistance. Here’s how a trendy Canadian retailer is dealing with the tariffs, and the origins of the “elbows up” movement.

Also, some Canadians want the government to get out of its deal with the U.S. to buy as many as 88 F-35s. And why not? This week, Vice President JD Vance called Canada “a state” during a speech in Maine.

When Mr. Carney ordered his negotiators to walk away, he did something that no other world leader has been able to do: stand up to Mr. Trump despite the risks.

Tuesday’s episode of “The Daily” explored why Canada is done with the U.S. president.

The Times’s chief White House correspondent, Peter Baker, wrote that while the president remains the most dominant figure in the world, other leaders and institutions are pushing back more vigorously than at the beginning of his second term.

As journalists, we’re always asking questions, especially during a relentless news cycle. We’re inviting you to send us your questions about the trade war, and our reporters will answer a selection in next week’s Canada Letter. Please email us at nytcanada@nytimes.com and include your full name and where you live.

We won’t publish your question without following up with you first, verifying your information and hearing back from you. And we won’t share your contact information outside the Times newsroom or use it for any reason other than to get in touch with you.

Thousands of Times readers shared reflections on the escalating trade war throughout the week. Here are just a few:

Assessing the characters of the US president and Canadian PM should give everyone serious pause before the mid-terms. CHARACTER MATTERS.

As a Canadian, I'm glad to see our prime minister standing firm. Three things are clear when dealing with Trump: any concessions will only provoke demands for more; he can't be trusted to honour any deal he makes; and his power is on the wane. The only smart option is to wait him out.

Canada has a stable, intelligent and thoughtful leader with a moral compass. We have Trump and Howard Lutnick. Is it any surprise that the US position was unstable? Instability is our motto now.

I’m a French Canadian from Quebec…never been more proud of being Canadian! Donald Trump was successful in 1 thing…uniting Canada like never before!

I’m not exactly young, and in all of my years, I never imagined that the greatest international threat to Canada as a nation would come from the United States. That country is not an ally, not a friend, but has in fact become an enemy. There is no other way to describe it.

The adults have arrived.

Jane Bradley, The Times’s new investigative reporter in Canada, and Michael Schwirtz, our global intelligence reporter, published an investigation this week showing that Russia is the largest destination for stolen Canadian cars, and how smugglers are meeting the demand of a booming black market.

Canadian universities announced the hiring of 64 international researchers, most of them from the United States, as part of a federally funded push to attract the world’s top academic talent, wrote Vjosa Isai, our reporter in Toronto.

Artemis Ghasemzadeh, who had escaped religious persecution, was deported to Panama under Trump’s immigration crackdown. Now, Canada has given her asylum.

Two rock climbers in British Columbia were rescued by helicopter after one of them was attacked by wasps and stung more than 100 times.

The police in Toronto are investigating after two cars were burned at the residence of a Liberal politician.

An airport services worker died after an accident at Montréal-Trudeau International Airport.

How are we doing?We’re eager to have your thoughts about this newsletter and events in Canada in general. Please send them to nytcanada@nytimes.com.

item.title: Why Iceland and Others Might Want In, Not Out, of the E.U. Club
item.description:
If Iceland votes on Saturday to restart talks to join the European Union, it will join a long list of hopefuls.

Ukraine sees membership as a security guarantee against Russia. Moldova wants in, as do Montenegro, Albania, Serbia and North Macedonia, among others. European officials even joke about adding Canada — which is, of course, not in Europe — to the mix.

Despite Britain’s not-so-silent exit in 2020, interest in boring, bureaucratic Brussels is strong thanks to Russian aggression, Chinese competition and Washington’s unpredictability.

“When the U.K. left the union, there was this moment where people were holding their breath: Would there be a domino effect?” said Almut Möller, the head of the program Europe in the World at the European Policy Center, a think tank.

Instead, becoming part of a like-minded group is now seen as “actually of great value,” she said, “if we are returning to a world of great power competition.”

Iceland’s vote will not be the final word on the European Union’s appeal — or lack thereof. Globally, critics continue to blast the sprawling system, its regulations and its rules. Icelanders remain split over whether they should throw themselves into talks.

What the European Union seems to offer prospective members is strength in numbers in a time of realpolitik.

Magnus Arni Skjold Magnusson, the chairman of the European Movement in Iceland, described the choice, in part, as a vote on values, as the United States pulls out of treaties, rolls back rights and courts corruption.

“Do we want to lean toward a nation, a country that doesn’t share our values on democracy, equality, gay rights?” Dr. Magnusson said. “Or do we want to align ourselves with like-minded nations?”

Iceland’s referendum will not determine whether it joins the European Union — that would take another vote. It will allow the Nordic nation to resume negotiations with the union on potential membership after more than a decade-long pause. Iceland tried to join the European Union after the mid-2000s global financial crisis but stopped the process amid industry opposition and grinding negotiations.

Iceland is already closely linked to the union and is a member of the free-movement Schengen area, allowing travelers to move between the island and other members without border checks. Joining the bloc could enable Iceland to opt into the euro, which appears to many in the country to be an enticingly stable currency.

Saturday’s vote comes as Russia has stepped up its activity in Arctic seas and after President Trump this year threatened to forcibly annex Greenland — and repeatedly mixed up “Iceland” and “Greenland” in a speech about that push.

“It feels like our neighborhood is being threatened,” said Edda Kentish, a 42-year-old Icelandic copywriter, who plans to vote yes on restarting the talks.

Joining the European Union could have costs for Iceland. The fishing industry has warned of increased competition. Others worry that Iceland will cede some of its sovereignty — or have its voice drowned out — if it joins the bloc.

“As the saying goes, if it’s not broken, don’t mess with it,” Kolbeinn Helgi Kristjansson, 33, who works in tourism, wrote in an email.

With fewer than 400,000 people, Iceland would be the smallest E.U. country. Germany’s population, for instance, is about 200 times larger.

Haraldur Olafsson, one of Iceland’s most vocal opponents of E.U. membership, said the bloc’s laws were made to fit Germany and France, and would expand regulations in his country. “You will be forced to use your money on all sorts of stupid things,” he said.

And adding new E.U. members is not easy — or fast. Brussels has been moving through negotiations with candidate countries slowly, to avoid allowing nations in too quickly or without sufficient guardrails.

Ukraine has been pushing for rapid membership, and E.U. officials often talk about the importance of bringing it in, but its candidacy is in fairly early stages. Montenegro has been trying to join since 2008, Albania since 2009. Turkey has formally been a candidate for membership in the union for decades, though its lack of progress toward E.U. standards has stalled its bid.

Adding poorer members can be expensive for member states, which end up funneling money toward integrating those economies. Beyond that, new members can bring added economic competition once they are more integrated into Europe’s shared market.

Nations that go on to elect governments with different goals and values than those that prevail in Brussels can slow joint decision-making.

Even with those concerns, Iceland might join relatively easily, given its close existing ties, high income and relatively stable political system. Marta Kos, the E.U. commissioner for enlargement, said this week that it could finalize negotiations in “one to two years.”

“I think this is a great time for Iceland to join because of the geopolitical situation we’re in,” Kristrun Frostadottir, Iceland’s prime minister, recently said on the podcast “The Rest Is Politics: Leading.” She said the union’s push to tighten alliances could give her nation a stronger negotiating position.

“They’re looking strategically around,” she added of the bloc. “They’re aware the world is changing.”

item.title: Tensions Spike Between Turkey and Israel as They Vie for Regional Influence
item.description:
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey has in recent years referred to Israel as a “terror state,” compared its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, to Hitler and suggested the possibility of Turkish military intervention inside Israel.

Mr. Netanyahu, for his part, has called Mr. Erdogan an “antisemitic dictator,” and members of the Israeli government have accused Turkey of supporting terrorism and acting like “an enemy state.”

This war of words is the most visible feature of a growing rivalry between Turkey and Israel that analysts and officials fear could exacerbate volatility in the Middle East, a region already reeling from wars and their aftermath in Syria, Lebanon, Gaza and Iran.

Both Turkey and Israel are allies of the United States and have warm relations with the Trump administration. But the countries, boasting strong militaries that are increasingly active outside their borders, are pursuing strategic visions that put them at odds in the Middle East, the Horn of Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean.

The heightened military assertiveness by Turkey and Israel has fueled “an inevitable geostrategic competition and rivalry,” said Ziya Meral, the director of Raven Research and Advisory, a global risk consultancy in London.

That does not mean the two countries will end up in open conflict, he said, but he warned that tension increased the risk of miscalculation and that limited military action by one side to “send a message” to the other “could really, really backfire.”

Israel made just such a move last week, when it bombed a defunct air base in northern Syria to pre-empt what Israeli officials said was the imminent deployment there of Turkish forces. Syria sits between Israel and Turkey, and both consider it crucial to their respective security.

The Turkish and Syrian governments denied plans for any such troop movement to the air base. No one was killed in the attack.

Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria and Iraq, criticized the strike in a post on social media as an “unnecessary escalation” and called on Turkey and Israel to “prioritize logical discourse over further military incidents.”

Relations between Turkey and Israel have not always been so bad. They have long had diplomatic and trade relations despite occasional disputes, usually related to Israel’s conflict with the Palestinians.

Turkey was the first Muslim-majority country to recognize Israel after its founding in 1948, and Turkish forces did not participate in the subsequent wars with Israel. Turkey is a U.S. ally in NATO, and Israel receives extensive military support from the United States.

Two recent events, however, have driven the relationship’s acrimonious turn.

The first was Israel’s war in Gaza, launched in response to the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed about 1,200 people in Israel. Turkish officials criticized how Israel fought in Gaza and routinely accused Israeli forces of committing genocide. Mr. Erdogan called Mr. Netanyahu a “bloodsucking vampire” and voiced support for Hamas, which Israel, the United States and other governments consider a terrorist organization.

The second event was the ouster of the dictator Bashar al-Assad in Syria in late 2024 and the creation of a new government headed by President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former jihadist with strong ties to Turkey.

Turkey has provided Mr. al-Sharaa with diplomatic and military support aimed at stabilizing his fragile state. In the wake of Mr. al-Assad’s ouster, meanwhile, Israeli strikes destroyed much of Syria’s military equipment, citing distrust of Mr. al-Sharaa. Israel has also occupied territory in southern Syria, saying this aims to prevent cross-border threats from Islamic militants.

The Hamas-led attack in 2023 shaped Israel’s approach to the region and to Turkey, said Gallia Lindenstrauss, a senior research fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv.

“We do not allow threats to grow; we tackle them in the beginning,” she said. “That’s the leading security doctrine, and that makes Israel more willing to take risks and less open to political settlements.”

Israel views Turkey as a growing military power with a weapons industry that competes in some markets against Israel’s, with troop deployments in other countries — including, in part, Syria and Iraq — and with leaders who speak of Israel in a hostile fashion, she said.

“When you have an actor that has capabilities and is talking in a certain way and is also showing its willingness to employ its forces beyond its borders, that’s something hard to ignore,” she said.

Recent events have also shaped Turkey’s approach to Israel.

Turkish leaders see a humanitarian catastrophe in the war in Gaza, which the enclave’s health authorities say has killed 73,000 people, including tens of thousands of women and children and an undisclosed number of militants. Turkish officials have called Israel’s military advances in Lebanon and Syria destabilizing.

Turkey also strongly opposed the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, saying it would provoke a dangerous regional crisis, and sought to prevent it.

Disagreements in the Middle East color interactions between the two countries elsewhere, said Salim Cevik, a visiting fellow at the Center for Applied Turkish Studies in Berlin.

“Because Turkey and Israel consider themselves rivals in the region, they consider each other’s movements in other places also from a win-and-lose perspective,” he said.

In the Horn of Africa, Turkey has a close relationship with Somalia, which hosts a substantial Turkish diplomatic and military presence.

In December, Israel became the first nation to recognize Somaliland, a breakaway region that declared independence from Somalia in 1991. At the time, Israel said the move was in line with the Abraham Accords, Israel’s recent normalization of relations with a few other Muslim-majority states. Mr. Erdogan called Israel’s recognition of Somaliland “illegal and unacceptable.”

In the Eastern Mediterranean, Israel has stepped-up military and energy cooperation with Greece and Cyprus, both of which have longstanding territorial disputes with Turkey. Mr. Erdogan sought to play down the importance of new agreements between the three countries in December, comparing them to “a rattling tin can.”

This month, Turkey signed a mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, which analysts said was partly intended to create a counterweight to Israeli influence in the region.

The rivalry’s most perilous flashpoint, however, remains Syria.

Turkey seeks a stable, centralized Syria, Mr. Cevik said, while Israel prefers a divided state with a weak military that cannot pose a threat.

“These two visions conflict very fundamentally,” he said.

The Israeli strike last week on the Syrian air base, in the town of Abu al-Duhur about 40 miles south of the Turkish border, was a rare military act in a competition that has largely played out in harsh statements and rival diplomatic initiatives.

On Aug. 19, the day after the strike, Mr. Netanyahu said in a video posted on social media that Israel would not accept a Turkish military presence in Syria “that descends south because it threatens us.”

Two days later, Turkey announced that it would seek the arrest of Mr. Netanyahu through Interpol on charges including genocide and torture as part of a domestic case in Turkey over Israel’s treatment of pro-Palestine activists intercepted at sea on their way to Gaza.

In the days since, U.S. officials have worked to restore dialogue between the two governments. Some Israeli analysts have speculated that the attack in Syria was part of an effort by Mr. Netanyahu to shore up his national security credentials ahead of Israeli elections in October.

Israel and Turkey are each unpopular among people in the other country, allowing officials to earn political points at home by criticizing the rival country.

Still, Mr. Cevik said, the heated language represents real disagreements.

He, too, said he did not expect Turkey and Israel to engage in direct military clashes.

“I don’t see it as likely because, primarily, the Americans have an interest in keeping these two countries away from active conflict,” he said.

David M. Halbfinger contributed reporting from Jerusalem, and Safak Timur from Istanbul.

item.title: Modi Is Hedging Against Trump, One Deal at a Time
item.description:
France. New Zealand. The Seychelles. Malaysia. Slovakia. Italy.

In the past year, Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India has zigzagged around the world at a breathless pace, pursuing new partners or bolstering ties with existing ones, jolted into action by a grim reality: India’s only way to combat the global turbulence unleashed by President Trump and fortify its economy is to spread its bets widely.

Since August 2025, Mr. Modi has paid official visits to at least 20 countries, and is set to visit more in the coming days, including a trip to Uzbekistan that starts on Saturday. Many of these meetings have been businesslike, resembling the urgent, closed-door discussions of Wall Street bankers negotiating deals.

After Uzbekistan, Mr. Modi will visit Kyrgyzstan for the annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a 10-member regional security group, where he is expected to sit down with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

Among the economic benefits for India that Mr. Modi has scored in his meetings are submarine technology from Germany, student visas from France, and cheaper Scotch whisky — arguably India’s most popular alcoholic beverage — from the United Kingdom.

“We want to build better ties with the rest of the world as the size of our economy grows,” said Priyam Gandhi-Mody, an executive director of the Future Economic Cooperation Council, an initiative of the government of Maharashtra, a western Indian state. She described India’s approach as “plurilateral” — pursing “smaller goals, more targeted goals and a smaller set of countries, until the time that goal is achieved.”

Many so-called middle powers — countries like France and Canada — have been kneecapped by the same forces India faces, making them more amenable to Mr. Modi’s overtures. Some are seeking him out to meet their own strategic needs and to get access to the world’s fastest-growing large economy.

India’s recalibrated approach to foreign policy made its debut about a year ago, following the 25 percent global tariffs Mr. Trump announced in February. The Trump administration began calling India out for its protectionist economy, and last August Mr. Trump slapped India with an additional 25 percent tariff for buying Russian oil, saying the purchases were helping finance its war in Ukraine.

During Mr. Trump’s first term, he and Mr. Modi cultivated a personal relationship that India expected to yield dividends. But New Delhi’s mood soured after Mr. Trump claimed repeatedly that he played a role in ending a four-day conflict between India and Pakistan in May 2025.

India has since rushed to find new partners to minimize the economic hit, as the United States was its largest single export market, as well as to strengthen relationships with countries like Japan and Australia that want to contain China in the Indo-Pacific region. The Iran war has made India’s mission only more urgent: With 80 percent of its crude oil imports coming through the Strait of Hormuz, it has been forced to find other transport routes.

Since December, Mr. Modi, 75, has visited 18 countries, but India’s dance card has filled up, too: The leaders of 13 countries have visited India.

Many such meetings produced specific agreements:

India and France have developed an especially close partnership, centered on artificial intelligence and governance, and on doubling bilateral trade within the next five years.

Mr. Modi and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, reaffirmed Norway’s commitment to creating one million jobs in India under an agreement India signed in October with the European Free Trade Association.

President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea promised investment in India and shipbuilding assistance. India aims to become one of the world’s top five shipbuilders by 2047.

Mr. Modi became the first Indian prime minister to visit New Zealand in four decades. The meeting focused on maritime security, building on a defense cooperation agreement signed last year, and doubling bilateral trade.

India signed a major free trade agreement with the European Union, the world’s largest economic bloc, in January. Roughly two decades of trade negotiations had been sped up by the newly upended world order.

India’s priorities can be grouped into thematic categories: defense technology; regional security; energy imports; critical minerals; artificial intelligence; and the ability of its people to study and work abroad, based on a review of its recent agreements.

Broadly, they reflect India and its partners’ goal of creating well-functioning economic corridors within which they can build resilience to future geopolitical shocks, analysts said. To maintain its “strategic autonomy” — a favored foreign policy stance — Mr. Modi has pursued economic diplomacy.

Many of the pacts underscore India’s need for support to create manufacturing jobs and technology to drive its growth, analysts said. But India is also working with countries to build infrastructure and find new buyers for its pharmaceuticals, as the world’s biggest maker of generic drugs. Unlike the diffuse nature of many previous meetings with leaders, the recent partnerships are far more focused, outlining specific goals, targets and numbers.

The E.U. deal — which Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, labeled the “mother of all deals” — marked a move away from India’s longstanding policy of protectionism. As part of the agreement, India agreed to make concessions, including slashing tariffs on European cars and wine, among other products. In 2025, India also struck a deal with the United Kingdom, where the latter reduced tariffs on garments, and the former slashed duties on alcohol.

The India-U. S. relationship is in “flux” and lacks “strategic focus” at the moment, said Chietigj Bajpayee, a South Asia expert at Chatham House, a London-based think tank. Mr. Bajpayee compared a recent meeting between Mr. Modi and Mr. Trump on the sidelines of the G7 summit in France to a “one-off coffee” rather than a relationship-building step.

Without a dependable relationship with the United States, he said, “India is back to pursuing a strategy where it balances and manages its relationships with both smaller countries, middle powers like Canada and Japan, and the global powers, U.S. and China.”

But Mr. Modi is hardly one to shy away from advertising personal chemistry where he can, to the cheers of his fellow Indians. During a meeting with Giorgia Meloni, Italy’s prime minister, Mr. Modi presented her with a bag of Melody toffee, a popular Indian candy. That very day, shares of an unrelated company with a name similar to the candy maker that produces Melody shot up on the Indian stock market.

]]>

item.title: Icelanders Are Voting on E.U. Membership Talks. Here’s What to Know.
item.description:
Icelanders are voting on Saturday in a national referendum on whether to restart negotiations to join the European Union, a contentious choice that some see as an essential question about their national future.

Iceland is already closely tied to the 27-nation bloc and follows many of its laws. But many in the island nation of 400,000 people see the referendum as deciding between maintaining Iceland’s independence and seeking the stability and security that the bloc could offer. Polls have shown a near-even split in public opinion.

If Icelanders vote to resume talks, negotiators will work to hammer out a deal, which could take years. Icelanders would then vote again on whether to join the bloc officially as a member state.

Some Icelanders feel that the European Union would offer security in numbers at a time of geopolitical upheaval. Iceland sits at the threshold of the Arctic, where superpowers are vying for dominance. President Trump’s pursuit of Greenland has rattled many in Iceland. (Mr. Trump repeatedly confused “Iceland” and “Greenland” in a speech this year.)

Iceland is the only NATO member that does not have a military. Though the European Union is not a military alliance, it does have a mutual defense clause.

The world is volatile, said Edda Kentish, a 42-year-old Icelandic copywriter, who is voting yes to talks: “We’re small, and that’s not going to cut it now.”

Some Icelanders worry about their financial situation — and their country’s — with inflation stubbornly high.

Many fear that the country’s economy is vulnerable to global shocks because of its small size and its dependence on tourism. Many “yes” voters think that joining one of the biggest economies in the world would bring stability.

Some say they want to see what could happen in negotiations and to keep their options open.

“I’m voting yes because I would like to see what the negotiations hold,” said Bjarki Eiriksson, a 42-year-old teacher. He added that he would vote against joining the European Union in a second referendum if he was not satisfied with a deal.

Negotiations would inevitably be complex and touch on many issues. Fishing would be a major one: It’s a large part of Iceland’s economy, and many Icelanders are unwilling to cede any control over the nation’s waters or its industry to the European Union.

“No” voters say they see the European Union as a potential threat to the country’s sovereignty.

Gudmundur Brynjolfsson, 62, a deacon in the town of Thorlakshofn, said he was voting no because he was worried about giving up power to the European Union and creating distance between Icelanders and their decision makers.

“Icelanders can today casually reach out to those in power,” he said. On Facebook, he said, “people even tag the prime minister personally when they are protesting something.”

Some farmers and fishermen are worried that they could suffer under E.U. rules, in part because of increased competition from within the bloc. People in the fishing industry, a major part of the Icelandic economy, are worried it could lose control of fishing rights in waters around the country.

Kolbeinn Helgi Kristjansson, 33, the chief executive of a northern lights tourism company, acknowledged that the European Union could bring economic benefits to some people. But he said Iceland could, overall, lose more from the bloc than it would gain, by giving away its powers.

“It’s like giving someone your lease and just hoping that they’ll treat you right,” he said.

If the referendum passes, Iceland and the European Union will begin negotiations on membership, known as accession. (Technically, this would be a resumption of talks — Iceland started negotiations after the global financial crisis but stopped them over a decade ago.)

Negotiations would inevitably be complex and touch on many issues. Fishing would probably be a major sticking point, though some Icelanders have been heartened by signs that the European Union might be willing to compromise on fishing quotas if it meant bringing Iceland into the bloc.

Any talks could take years. If there is a deal, Icelanders will then vote in another referendum on whether to join the European Union as a member state. There would be other steps: Political leaders would need to approve the agreement, and the Icelandic Constitution would need to be amended before the country could join the bloc.

If the referendum fails, Iceland will not start talks with the bloc at this time. It is still possible that Iceland will try to join in the future, but experts say the result would most likely chill efforts to reopen the debate for many years.

Most polls close at 10 p.m. local time on Saturday (6 p.m. Eastern time).

The first numbers will probably start to come in as early as 10:30 p.m. local time (6:30 p.m. Eastern) on Saturday, according to RUV, Iceland’s national broadcaster.

Although the country’s six constituencies are expected to release their own results throughout the night, the National Electoral Commission plans to release the nationwide result around 12 p.m. local time on Sunday (8 a.m. Eastern).

Egill Bjarnason contributed reporting from Husavik, Iceland.

]]>

item.title: Carney Has Canadians’ Support on Trump. Now Comes the Hard Part.
item.description:
When Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada addressed the nation a week ago, hours after walking away from trade talks with the United States, he invited 41 million Canadians into the negotiating room.

They overwhelmingly rallied behind his nerve, which, Mr. Carney said, avoided “a bad deal” that would have put Canada’s sovereignty in the hands of the man who wants to make the country the 51st American state.

Public support allowed Mr. Carney to negotiate fiercely; and it carried him through a high-risk moment for the country’s economy as he suspended the talks.

Walking away is a typical negotiating move, usually deployed to break through an impasse and arm the departing party with an advantage. The point is to start again from a better position.

So when the time comes to reopen trade talks with the United States, the enthusiastic public support that has buttressed Mr. Carney’s choices has the potential to become an obstacle. He will need to somehow tap into Canadians’ pragmatism and understanding of the economic predicament the country will face if the trade war with the United States goes on. And even so, there is a risk that many of them, angered and defiant today, could feel misled if a return to talks is not handled with care.

Before President Trump set off a global eye-roll by signing an executive order on Thursday afternoon to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” the first sign of de-escalation in the frayed U.S.-Canada relationship had started to show.

In an interview on Wednesday with the CBC, Canada’s national broadcaster, Jamieson Greer, the United States’ trade representative, said that demands raised by the U.S. side during discussions about the promotion of Canadian content on U.S. online streaming platforms had not been a deal breaker.

The next day, Dominic LeBlanc, a senior Canadian cabinet minister who played a leading role in the talks, welcomed Mr. Greer’s comment, cautiously putting a toe back in the water.

“We look forward to further constructive U.S. clarifications on their other positions which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty,” he said in a statement.

It was, perhaps, too soon.

Mere hours later, Mr. Trump signed his executive order renaming Lake Ontario and called Canadian leadership “nasty.”

Officials from both sides have said they’re not currently talking, and it is clear that, for any conversation to restart in earnest, a cooling-off period will be needed, and the next few months will provide a map for when talks may restart.

Canada’s countertariffs against U.S. goods are set to take effect on Sept. 8, while a further round of U.S. levies announced by Mr. Trump, which will further raise existing tariffs against Canadian goods such as automobiles and steel, will begin on Jan. 1. The U.S. midterm elections in November also present an opportunity for Mr. Carney, who has targeted countertariffs on U.S. products with swing states in mind.

A seasoned negotiator from his days in finance, Mr. Carney is unlikely to wait to return to the table when the Canadian economy has begun to show real signs of strain. The months ahead will be hard for Canadians. In the case of industries already under tariffs since last year — steel, aluminum, softwood lumber, autos and automobile parts — the protracted and escalating trade war means more unemployment and uncertainty.

Mr. Carney’s government has acknowledged this pain, and announced plans to mitigate some of it. In the meantime, the Canadian economy is showing good vital signs: On Friday, it registered a 3.3 percent growth rate in the second quarter of the year, the fastest since early 2023.

Additionally, the public’s resolve for Canada to stand its ground against the Trump administration appears solid.

“I’ve been looking at this data for a long time, and people have been unequivocal and clear: We’ve had majorities now for more than a year, saying we should take a tough approach, we should take a hard line, we should not give away too much,” said Shachi Kurl, who leads the Angus Reid Institute, a nonpartisan public opinion research organization in Canada.

Polling released soon after the talks collapsed showed that three-quarters of Canadians backed Mr. Carney’s decision.

Returning to trade talks given all that has transpired will require Canadians to hold two truths at once: Alongside their genuine, heightened patriotism in the face of Mr. Trump’s tariffs and his menacing rhetoric toward Canada, they will need to also be pragmatic about the economic reality the country faces as the trade war takes hold.

That pragmatism will be necessary if Mr. Carney can count on the broad support he has today to return to talks with the United States and see if he can get a better deal than the one he left on the table.

“Canadians are completely aware that this is the most important economic relationship that we have,” Ms. Kurl said. “There is absolutely pragmatism there.”

Polling shows that Canadians are concerned about the economy and their jobs, just as they are asking Mr. Carney to stick up for them.

Much of how Mr. Carney’s negotiating position plays out will come down to his ability to guide public opinion as he makes the case for giving trade talks another chance.

“He will have to come back and say: ‘Look, if that was the right thing to do then, this is the right thing to do now. Stick with me, trust me,’” Mr. Kurl said.

item.title: 27 Killed Near Kyiv as Russian Drone Blitz Exposes Air Defense Gap
item.description:
For several terrifying days, air raid sirens have wailed nonstop in Kyiv, Ukraine’s capital, as waves upon waves of armed Russian drones surged into the city, straining its limited air defenses and exhausting a population worn down by years of war.

This latest stage of Russia’s air campaign has targeted warehouses and shopping centers, and on Saturday, the Ukrainian authorities said that a strike on a facility just outside Kyiv had killed at least 27 people.

The strike, which took place late Friday, caused huge secondary explosions that engulfed an entire suburban area in plumes of smoke. The Ukrainian authorities did not say what the facility was, but their comments suggested it was a warehouse with ammunition.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said on Saturday that a criminal investigation was already underway into the management of the warehouse, which is near private homes and a facility for older adults and people with disabilities.

An ammunition depot in another area outside Kyiv was destroyed last month, killing several people and prompting a separate investigation into the decision to store dangerous arms in civilian areas.

“Making the same mistakes for the fifth year of the full-scale invasion is criminal negligence,” Serhii Koretskyi, Ukraine’s prime minister, said on Saturday. “And all those responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations do not happen again.”

Ukraine is struggling to counter the onslaught of Russian drones, many of which are powered by jet engines that allow them to fly at nearly 400 miles an hour.

The latest drone campaign has coincided with Ukraine’s dire shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles, the only weapon the country has that can shoot down ballistic missiles.

Russia has seized on that gap in Ukraine’s arsenal this summer. Civilians are bracing for the possibility that waves of Russian drones are intended to wear down air defense units before an even larger ballistic attack in the coming days.

In the past, Russia often launched daytime waves of reconnaissance drones ahead of combined drone and missile attacks overnight. But the droves of armed drones that now swarm the capital daily suggest that Russia is using a new tactic to spread fear and anxiety.

Most shops and restaurants remain open in Kyiv, but the constant attacks have caused major traffic jams and delays on the metro system. They could also significantly complicate plans for students to return to school on Tuesday.

item.title: ‘Immense’ Devastation as Nepal Continues Search for 2,400 Missing in Floods
item.description:
Entire towns wiped out. Roads, bridges and communication lines washed away. In just a matter of moments, tens of thousands of people were left devastated and disoriented as catastrophic floodwaters tore through the tranquil Himalayan valley.

Four days later, as the rescue efforts in Nepal and neighboring Tibet continued on Saturday, the staggering scale of the flood’s devastation was coming into focus.

The official count of missing people jumped to over 2,400, more than double the figure from a day before. The death toll rose to over 600 and was expected to keep climbing. The morgues in several of the towns downstream from the deluge have been overwhelmed by the number of bodies, with officials forced to improvise makeshift arrangements.

“In living memory, we haven’t seen a mountain hazard event like this,” Kamal Kishore, the United Nations’ top official for disaster risk reduction, said on Friday. “The impact on lives, livelihoods, buildings, infrastructure, bridges, hydroelectric projects, power generation is really immense.”

The recovery will be daunting.

Nepal is one of the poorest countries in the world. Its economy, long stagnated, is heavily reliant on the tourism industry and the remittances its workers send from abroad.

The small Himalayan nation also remains one of the most susceptible to climate change. Scientists have long warned about potential flooding from the lakes that melting glaciers have formed in the mountains. Even in normal years, smaller floods related to monsoon rains cause mudslides and block roads, straining the country’s vulnerable infrastructure.

The threat of fresh flooding hangs heavy over the rescue and relief efforts.

China reported on Friday that a barrier lake, created when the landslide that started Wednesday’s deluge blocked the river system, had begun overflowing in Tibet, near where the floods originated. Nepali authorities issued repeated alerts downstream, and police officers hurried through nearby towns with megaphones, asking people to move to higher ground.

Much of the rescue effort on the Nepali side of the border appeared focused on several hydropower plants that were swept away by the torrent of water and debris. Army rescue teams rushed to recover workers from the muddy tunnels in dramatic scenes.

In a sign of how uncertain the situation remained, hundreds of workers from those plants had not been counted among the initial missing tally, Nepali officials said in explaining the sudden jump in the number of missing.

The threat of flooding temporarily paused the rescue efforts in Tibet on Friday. But on Saturday, Chinese rescue workers resumed their search efforts, looking for survivors near the Gyirong border crossing between Nepal and Tibet, China’s state broadcaster, CCTV, reported. The footage showed firefighters combing the leveled site, tapping on the ground with shovels and shouting, “Is anyone there?”

The government in Nepal, which swept to power earlier this year on the back of Gen Z protests, is trying to assert control and restore order in the face of the overwhelming tragedy.

Balendra Shah, the 36-year-old prime minister, has not addressed the nation but has been seen visiting the sites of destruction and leading meetings to coordinate the country’s response.

His government has deployed over 30,000 security forces for rescue and recovery efforts. Possibly drawing on lessons from the response to a previous natural disaster in the country, which was criticized as chaotic and disorganized, the authorities this week initially declined foreign rescue teams. But by the end of Friday, news media in Nepal reported that the government was easing that restriction.

Thousands of people have been rescued so far, many of them pulled out of flooded villages in helicopters before being sent to hospitals and relief camps, where they have been given meals and medical help.

Soon, the focus will have to shift to rebuilding. But for those who survived the surging waters — losing loved ones, livelihoods and homes — a path to recovery may seem distant. It is unclear whether many survivors will be able to return home or if they will need to resettle elsewhere.

The damage has also been particularly heavy at the site of hydropower projects built along the Bhotekoshi and other rivers downstream. Tens of miles of roads and over 40 bridges have been destroyed.

Initial government estimates in Nepal have put the cost of physical damage at over $1.3 billion, and the country’s finance minister has predicted that recovery efforts could run into “a few billions.”

Anupreeta Das and Lily Kuo contributed reporting.
